site.title: The Quesenberry & Harvey Family
site.subtitle: An American Story
site.tagline: Four centuries from the Virginia Tidewater to the Carolina Piedmont
site.intro: From the wooden ships that crossed the Atlantic in 1624, to the Highland Scots who landed at Wilmington in 1775, to the Confederate soldiers of Floyd County and the Wesleyan congregations of High Point — this is the chronicle of two families whose stories braid into the larger story of America itself.

narrative: Lonnie Olin Quesenberry was born on the 18th of March, 1920, in **Kingsport, Sullivan County, Tennessee** — in the far northeast corner of that state, where the Holston River runs out of southwestern Virginia and the Cumberland Gap is one ridge over. The Quesenberry family had been in the Floyd County, Virginia mountains for five generations; by Lonnie's birth they had drifted south and west, across the state line, into the new industrial town of Kingsport (which had been incorporated only three years before, in 1917, as a planned community around a Mead pulp-and-paper mill).

His father, **Floyd Harmon Quesenberry**, was thirty-five when Lonnie was born; his mother, **Eva Elizabeth Mullins**, was twenty-eight. Lonnie had at least one sibling — **Billie R. Quesenberry** — who appears alongside him in the 1940 federal census household, both still children at home. By 1935 the family had moved again, this time east to **Western Branch, Norfolk, Virginia** — five miles from the great Naval Operating Base, where the buildup to the Second World War would soon make work plentiful for any able-bodied young man with mechanical aptitude.

Lonnie turned twenty-one in March 1941, nine months before Pearl Harbor. On 16 July of that year he is recorded in a Norfolk newspaper. His **WWII Draft Registration Card**, since recovered, was filed at Bowers Hill, Norfolk, Virginia — the Naval shipyard country. Whether he served at sea or worked the yards through the war years is not yet known; the National Archives service record will tell the rest of that story.

By 1949 Lonnie was settled in Greensboro, North Carolina — newly married. On the 17th of July, 1948 — when the country was rebuilding itself from the war — Lonnie had married **Ruth Garland Harvey** in Greensboro. He was 28; she was 23, valedictorian of Colfax High School a few years before.

Together they raised three children — Phillip Olyn, Cathey Arlene, and Carol Jeanette — in High Point, the furniture-making capital of the South. He died on the 22nd of December, 2002, at the age of 82, in High Point Care Center, and was buried at Holly Hill Memorial Park in Thomasville. His wife of fifty-four years would lie beside him fourteen years later.

narrative: Ruth Garland Harvey was born on the 27th of June, 1925, in Guilford County, North Carolina — daughter of **William Carl Harvey** (1887–1966) and **Geneva Esther McMicheal Harvey** (1891–1971). Both were of the Piedmont North Carolina farming families that had been working the rolling Guilford red clay for generations.

She grew up in Colfax, a small farming community west of Greensboro that had been called "Dover" before the 1800s and was first settled by families coming south from Pennsylvania and Virginia. There, at Colfax High School, she earned the highest distinction her school could grant: she was named *valedictorian* of her graduating class — the top student in her year. In a small, rural Piedmont school in the 1940s, this was no small thing.

She was, the obituary remembered, *"an excellent self-taught cook"* — the highest compliment in a Southern family. She married Lonnie Olin Quesenberry on the 17th of July, 1948, in Greensboro, and together they made a home in High Point. She joined the Greenwood Hills Wesleyan Church on North Main Street, a congregation in the Wesleyan-Methodist tradition that had broken from the larger Methodist body in 1843 over the question of slavery — a denomination that prided itself, even into the twentieth century, on plain living and quiet conviction.

Ruth outlived her husband by fourteen years and her son Phil by one. When she died on the 21st of January, 2016, at Shannon Gray Health Care, she left behind two daughters, six grandchildren, eleven great-grandchildren, and one great-great-grandchild — a small republic of descendants stretching across the Carolinas and beyond.

narrative: Esther Harvey Scott was born on the 2nd of August, 1929, in Colfax, the small farming community of western Guilford County, NC, to Carol and Geneva Harvey — Ruth Garland Harvey's parents. She was Ruth's younger sister by four years and one month.

On the 9th of August 1947 — about eleven months before Ruth's own wedding — Esther married **Anderson L. Scott**. They settled in Kernersville, in adjacent Forsyth County. Esther trained as a Licensed Practical Nurse and spent her working life caring for patients: as a private-duty nurse in homes around Kernersville, then on the wards of Forsyth Memorial Hospital, and finally as office nurse for Dr. Leo Record in Kernersville. She remained a homemaker through it all.

Like her sister, she carried her parents' Wesleyan faith into her adult life. Where Ruth attended Greenwood Hills Wesleyan Church in High Point, Esther worshiped at **Shady Grove Wesleyan Church** back in her birthplace of Colfax — and there, in the Shady Grove churchyard, she was buried after several months of decline, on the 3rd of February 2021. She had outlived her older sister by five years.

Esther's published obituary is, on the present record, the single most important documentary source for the Harvey side of this family — it is what gave us her parents' first names, her birthplace, her birth date, her wedding date and husband, and her burial place. Without it, the Harvey-Carmichael line would still be no more than the four words "Carl Harvey and Geneva Carmichael Harvey" from Ruth's own obituary.

narrative: **Floyd Harmon Quesenberry** was born in 1885, of the old Quesenberry line that had come down from Floyd County, Virginia — the mountain country named for Governor John Floyd, where Quesenberry families had been numerous since the eighteenth century. His father was **Alexander H. Quesenberry** (1863–1937), and his mother was **Matilda Jane Price** (1867–1944) — both of the southwestern Virginia uplands.

Sometime before 1920 Floyd married **Eva Elizabeth Mullins** (1891–1983) and moved south across the state line into Tennessee. Their son Lonnie was born in Kingsport, Sullivan County, Tennessee on 18 March 1920. A second son, Billie R., would follow. By the mid-1930s the family had relocated again — this time east to the Norfolk, Virginia shipyards, where work was plentiful for skilled men in the years before the Second World War.

Floyd lived to be eighty-five, dying in 1970. He had seen his son Lonnie marry, settle in High Point, and raise three children — Phil, Cathey, and Carol — to adulthood. The Quesenberry surname, planted on a wooden ship in 1624 and carried through nine American generations, had reached its third state and its tenth generation in his lifetime.

narrative: Eva Elizabeth Mullins was born in 1891, the daughter of **James C. C. Mullins** (most likely James Calaway "Cad/Cade" Mullins, 1854–1929) and **Annis Stapleton**. The Mullins surname is a famous one in southwestern Virginia and eastern Tennessee — perhaps most famous for the Melungeon Mullins families of Wise and Lee Counties, Virginia, though Eva's specific line has yet to be traced in detail.

She married **Floyd Harmon Quesenberry** before 1920 and bore him at least two sons — Lonnie Olin (1920) in Kingsport, Tennessee, and Billie R. Quesenberry. In the 1940 federal census the family is recorded at Western Branch, Norfolk, Virginia, and Eva appears as **"Evvie"** — the household name everyone called her by.
She lived to be ninety-two, dying in 1983. By then her son Lonnie had been married thirty-five years and her grandchildren were grown.

narrative: The first thing to settle about Lonnie's father-in-law is the simplest question: what was his name? Ruth's 2016 obituary called him **Carl**; Esther's 2021 obituary called him **Carol**. The Ancestry records resolve it: his full given name was **William Carl Harvey** — born 1887, died 25 November 1966 in Greensboro. *Carl* was the name he was called by; *William* the formal first; *Carol* was a phonetic spelling variant on Esther's obituary.

He married **Geneva Esther McMicheal** on the 20th of June, 1919, in Guilford County, North Carolina. He was thirty-two; she was twenty-seven. They settled in the Deep River area of Guilford County, where the federal censuses of 1930 and 1950 record their household. Their daughter **Ruth Garland Harvey** was born in June 1925; their second daughter **Esther** arrived four years later in August 1929.

He was the son of **Isaac J. Harvey** and **Rachel (Frances) Swift Harvey** — both names confirmed in the genealogical record. The Harveys had been Piedmont North Carolina farmers for at least three generations.

Carl raised his daughters in the Wesleyan Church — Ruth at Greenwood Hills Wesleyan in High Point, Esther at Shady Grove Wesleyan in Colfax — an unusual denomination in the otherwise Methodist and Baptist Piedmont. He died on the 25th of November, 1966, in Greensboro, age 79. Geneva would survive him by five years.

narrative: Geneva Esther McMicheal was born on the 5th of September, 1891, in North Carolina. *Earlier research called her maiden name Carmichael; the documentary record corrects that — her maiden name was* **McMichael** *(occasionally spelled McMicheal). The error matters: McMichael and Carmichael are distinct Scottish-derived surnames, and the entire Highland Scotland / Jupiter of Larne migration story we once told about this branch does not apply to your family. The McMichaels of Guilford County are their own line, with their own American story.*

Her father was **William Franklin McMichael** (1849–1941), of the Deep River community in Guilford County, North Carolina. Her mother was named **Sally Pegram** (born about 1860), though Find a Grave alternately identifies her mother as **Esther Jane McMichael** — a discrepancy worth resolving (Geneva's middle name *Esther* may well honor her mother). The 1900 federal census records her, age 8, in the household at Deep River.

On the 20th of June, 1919, she married **William Carl Harvey** in Guilford County. She was twenty-seven; he was thirty-two. They settled in Deep River, where the 1930 and 1950 censuses found them with their two daughters Ruth and Esther. Her father died on 3 April 1941 at Forsyth, NC, age 91 or 92.

Geneva outlived her husband by five years. She died on the 27th of February, 1971, at Winston-Salem in Forsyth County, age 79, and was buried in Colfax, Guilford County — where her daughter Esther would be buried fifty years later, at Shady Grove Wesleyan Church Cemetery.

william-henry-quesenberry.military: American Civil War — Confederate Army (one of the famous nine sons)
william-henry-quesenberry.epitaph: Born in a Blue Ridge hollow, named for a Whig statesman, fought for the Confederacy, died in the Arizona desert. One of nine brothers in the same gray uniform.

facts.Civil War: Confederate — one of the nine Quesenberry brothers

narrative: **William Henry Clay Quesenberry** — named for the great Kentucky Whig statesman who had been the most famous American politician of the previous quarter-century — was born on the 10th of January, 1842, in Indian Valley, in Floyd County, Virginia. He was a son of John Quesenberry Sr. and Nancy Hylton, the eighth or ninth of their fourteen children. He grew up in a great clamoring household of brothers — George Washington, Elijah, Thomas Frederick, Archelaus, Nathaniel Floyd, John Jr., his older brother William Henry Clay (yes, the family was named for politicians), Amos Ballard, James Montgomery, and the daughters who married into the Hylton, Slusher, and Cox families of the same Floyd County valleys.

He turned nineteen on the eve of the Civil War. Like the rest of his brothers — *all nine of them* — he enlisted in the Confederate Army. The Quesenberry family of John and Nancy is remembered in regional Civil War history as the only American family known to have sent **nine sons** into Confederate service. The 54th Virginia Infantry and Company G of the 49th Virginia Infantry both included Quesenberrys; the 1862 muster roll preserved in the Quesenberry Family Papers at the Virginia Museum of History & Culture in Richmond names them. (The Quesenberry sons fought variously at Murfreesboro, Chickamauga, and through the Atlanta Campaign.)

On the 15th of January, 1867 — barely two years after Appomattox — William Henry Clay married Eva Jane Slusher, of the German-American Slusher (originally Schlosser) family that had settled the same Floyd County valleys. Together they had at least six children — Sylvester Plane, Paulina, Nancy Ellender, Elkanah Abner, Alice Jane, and John William.

And then, late in life, he did the most American thing a mountain Virginian of his generation could do: he went west. He died in Glendale, Maricopa County, in the Arizona Territory, on the 6th of February, 1898 — the year *Maine* was sunk in Havana Harbor. He had crossed a continent. His widow Eva Jane lived another twenty-eight years.

eva-jane-slusher.epitaph: Granddaughter of a Pennsylvania-German DAR Patriot, daughter of the Slushers and the Hyltons of Indian Valley, wife of one of the nine Confederate Quesenberrys. She lived from Andrew Jackson to Calvin Coolidge.

facts.Father: Stephen Slusher (1800–1838) — died the year Eva was born
facts.Paternal grandfather: Christopher Slusher / Schlosser (1757–1845) — DAR Patriot Ancestor

narrative: Eva Jane Slusher was born on the 20th of January, 1838 — the same year her father, Stephen Slusher, died, and the same year her grandmother Eve Hancock died. She came into the world at the precise moment that two generations of her family departed it.

Her surname, *Slusher*, is the anglicized form of the German *Schlosser* — meaning *locksmith* — and it traces to the great wave of Pennsylvania-Dutch and Palatine German settlers who poured down the Great Wagon Road into the Virginia and Carolina backcountry in the eighteenth century.

Her paternal grandfather was **Christopher Slusher** (1757–1845), a verified Revolutionary War soldier and **DAR Patriot Ancestor #A105465**, who served from Pennsylvania during the American Revolution before settling in Floyd County. Her paternal grandmother was Eve (Eve Jane) Hancock (1761–1838) — the original *Eva Jane* whose name Eva would carry. Her mother **Charlotte Hylton** (1804–1894) was a daughter of Archelaus Hylton and Catharine Weddle, of the great Hylton clan that had been among the very first white families to settle Indian Valley.

Eva Jane married William Henry Clay Quesenberry on the 15th of January, 1867 — the year of his twenty-fifth birthday and the second January after Appomattox. Together they raised six children. She survived him by twenty-eight years, dying on the 17th of December, 1926. She had lived through the presidencies of Andrew Jackson, Abraham Lincoln, and Calvin Coolidge.

john-quesenberry-sr.name: John Quesenberry Sr.
john-quesenberry-sr.epitaph: Patriarch of Greasy Creek — and, by Civil War's end, the only American father documented to have sent nine sons into Confederate service.

facts.Children: 14 children — including nine sons in the Confederate Army

narrative: John Quesenberry Sr. was born in 1790 at Greasy Creek, in what would in 1831 become Floyd County, Virginia — one of those Blue Ridge valleys whose names (Greasy Creek, Indian Valley, Burks Fork) still feel like the frontier they were. He was the son of **George Quesenberry**, who had served in the Montgomery County, Virginia Militia during the American Revolution, and Martha 'Patsy' Slinker.

He married **Nancy Hylton** (1803 – after 1860), of the great Hylton family that had been among the very first white settlers of Indian Valley. Together they had fourteen children. The federal census of 1840 records their household at fourteen souls; by 1850 it numbered twelve, with ten children at home.

And then, in the year that John died — 1853 — the country slid toward the war that would define his sons' lives. When the Civil War came eight years later, **all nine of John's surviving sons enlisted in the Confederate Army**: George Washington Quesenberry, Elijah Quesenberry, Thomas Frederick Quesenberry, Archelaus Quesenberry, Nathaniel Floyd Quesenberry, John Quesenberry Jr., William Henry Clay Quesenberry, Amos Ballard Quesenberry, and James Montgomery Quesenberry. They served variously in the 54th Virginia Infantry, the 49th Virginia Infantry (Company G), and other regiments raised in the southwestern counties. The Quesenberry Family Papers at the Virginia Museum of History & Culture preserve the 1862 muster roll. **No other American family on documentary record sent nine sons into Confederate service.**
John Quesenberry Sr. did not live to see it. He died in Wythe County in 1853, and lies — by family tradition — somewhere in the high country between Greasy Creek and the New River.

george-quesenberry.military: American Revolutionary War — Montgomery County, Virginia Militia
narrative: George Quesenberry was born in 1748 in Orange County, Virginia, in the rich Piedmont west of the Tidewater settlements. He was a son of Aaron Quisenberry Sr. and Joyce Gayle Dudley — a third-generation American whose great-grandfather had crossed the Atlantic during the reign of King James I.

When the Revolution came, George served with the **Montgomery County, Virginia Militia** — one of the western militia units that defended the Virginia frontier during the war and that, on occasion, marched east to join the Continental Army or skirmish with Loyalists. The Montgomery County militia was active throughout the war, and Quesenberrys appear on its muster rolls.

After the Revolution, George followed the southwestern Virginia migration into the high country that would become Floyd County in 1831. He died there in 1812 — when the United States was at war with Britain a second time. His sons would clear and farm the same Greasy Creek and Indian Valley hollows that his great-great-grandsons would still be working a century later.

aaron-quisenberry.military: American Revolution — DAR Patriot Ancestor #A093307; furnished beef to the Continental Army
narrative: Aaron Quisenberry Sr. was born in 1725 in Caroline County, Virginia — when George I sat on the British throne and the colonies were still half a century away from independence. He married **Joyce Gayle Dudley** in King George County in 1741, when he was sixteen. Together they would have ten children over the next twenty-nine years.

When the American Revolution came, Aaron — by then a man in his fifties with grown sons of fighting age — supported the cause materially: he furnished beef from his Orange County farm to the Continental Army. This service is recognized by both the **Daughters of the American Revolution** and the **National Society Sons of the American Revolution**, which list him as a verified Patriot Ancestor. Any descendant of Aaron Quisenberry — and the Quesenberry family has many thousands of descendants — is therefore eligible for membership in the DAR or SAR through his line.
He died on the 11th of March, 1795, in St. Thomas Parish, Orange County, Virginia. His son George had already taken the family name into the Blue Ridge frontier.

thomas-questenbury.name: Thomas Questenbury
thomas-questenbury.epitaph: The Atlantic crossing of 1624 — Thomas Questenbury, sixteen years old, a passenger to colonial Virginia. From him every American Quesenberry, Quisenberry, and Christenberry descends.

facts.Generation: Colonial immigrant ancestor (~9 generations back from Lonnie)
facts.American descendants: All Quesenberry / Quisenberry families in the United States

narrative: On a wooden ship sometime in the year 1624, a sixteen-year-old boy named **Thomas Questenbury** sailed from the south of England — most likely from Gravesend or one of the Kentish ports — to the seventeen-year-old colony of Virginia. He had been born in 1608 in Bromley, in the county of Kent, the son of James Questenbury and Joan Lydes. The Jamestown settlement was barely a generation old when he stepped ashore.

He survived. He married in Virginia and fathered at least two sons — John and Francis — who remained in the colony and became the patriarchs of the American Quesenberry families. By 1650, Thomas appears to have returned to England, settling in Canterbury and contracting a second marriage there. He died at Canterbury in 1672, at the age of about sixty-four.

But his sons stayed. From his son **John Quisenberry** (1627–1717), born in colonial Virginia, the entire American Quesenberry/Quisenberry/Christenberry line descends — every Quesenberry in Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, Texas, and points west. The 1840 federal census found 71% of all Quesenberrys in America still living in Virginia. They all came from this one boy on a Kentish ship in 1624.

There is a poetic detail. Thomas Questenbury's American daughter-in-law, **Anne Pope** of Westmoreland County (whom his son John married after 1658), was a cousin of *another* Anne Pope — the Anne Pope who married Colonel John Washington, the great-grandfather of George Washington. The Quesenberrys and the Washingtons share a kinship through the Popes of Westmoreland County.

john-quisenberry-1627.name: John Quisenberry Sr.
john-quisenberry-1627.epitaph: First American-born Quisenberry — planter of Westmoreland County, husband of Anne Pope, by marriage a distant cousin of George Washington.

facts.Wife: Anne Pope (1629–1735), cousin of Anne Pope Washington

narrative: John Quisenberry was born in 1627 in colonial Virginia — three years after his father Thomas had stepped off the ship from Kent. He was, on the present record, the **first American-born Quesenberry**.

Sometime after 1658 he married **Anne Pope** of Westmoreland County, of the Pope family that had been planters in the Virginia Tidewater since the 1640s. The Anne Pope whom John Quisenberry married was a *cousin of another Anne Pope* — the Anne Pope who had married Colonel John Washington in 1658. Colonel Washington was the great-grandfather of President George Washington. The two Pope cousins worshiped at the same church and lived as neighbors in Westmoreland County. **Through this marriage the Quesenberrys and the Washingtons are distant kin** — a connection now verified through the National Park Service's biographical material on Anne Pope Washington and through corroborating Pope-family genealogies on WikiTree.

John was a wealthy planter. He owned large tracts in old Northumberland County (now Westmoreland), Virginia. His will, dated the 23rd of November 1714, was probated three years later, on the 27th of November 1717. He had three sons — John (who died childless), William (1672–1762), and Humphrey (d. before 1727) — and through William and Humphrey the American Quesenberry, Quisenberry, and Christenberry families fan out across the colonies and, eventually, the continent.

He lived to be about ninety. When he was born, Charles I sat on the English throne and Massachusetts was barely a colony. When he died, George I was on the British throne and the American population had crossed half a million.

christopher-slusher.name: Christopher Slusher (Schlosser)
christopher-slusher.military: American Revolution — DAR Patriot Ancestor #A105465 (Pennsylvania service)
christopher-slusher.epitaph: Revolutionary War soldier from Lancaster County, Pennsylvania — DAR Patriot Ancestor #A105465 — and the German-American great-grandfather of Eva Jane Slusher.
narrative: Christopher Slusher — born **Schlosser**, the family name still spelled in the original German — came into the world on the 15th of October, 1757, in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. He was the son of Pennsylvania-Dutch parents whose ancestors had crossed the Atlantic from the Palatinate and settled among the great Pennsylvania-German farming community of the early eighteenth century.

He was eighteen when the American Revolution began, and he served — he is recorded today as a verified **DAR Patriot Ancestor, #A105465**, with documented Revolutionary War service from Pennsylvania. The exact unit and dates are recorded in the DAR archives in Washington; a SAR application or DAR membership application through his line would surface the specific service record.

After the war, like many Pennsylvania-German families of his generation, he migrated south down the Great Wagon Road into the Virginia and Carolina backcountry. He married **Eve Hancock** (1761–1838), and together they raised a family in Floyd County, Virginia — the same Blue Ridge country where Christopher's grandsons and great-grandsons would marry into the Quesenberry, Hylton, and Cox families.

He lived to be eighty-eight, dying on the 11th of December, 1845, in Floyd County. His granddaughter Eva Jane Slusher would marry William Henry Clay Quesenberry twenty-two years after his death, joining the Slusher and Quesenberry lines that this site traces forward to Lonnie Olin Quesenberry.

He appears in the 1940 federal census household at Western Branch, Norfolk, Virginia, alongside Lonnie and their parents Floyd and 'Evvie' Quesenberry — listed as 'Billie R. Quesenberry'. narrative: **Pvt. Alexander Henry Quesenberry, Sr.** was born on the 6th of January, 1842, in Washington County, Virginia — the far southwest corner of the state, in the high mountain country bordering Tennessee. He was twenty when he married **Rebecca Jane Smyth** (1844–1920) in or around 1862. Whether they had even a year together as husband and wife is uncertain — what is certain is that by the spring of 1863 he was a Confederate Private somewhere in the Army of Northern Virginia, and Rebecca was carrying their first and only child.

On the **3rd of May, 1863**, he was killed at the **Battle of Chancellorsville**, in Spotsylvania County, Virginia — Robert E. Lee's greatest tactical victory, and the battle in which Stonewall Jackson was mortally wounded by his own men two nights before. Some 17,000 Union soldiers and 13,000 Confederates fell over those three days. Pvt. Alexander Henry Quesenberry was one of them, dead at age twenty-one.

His son, **Alexander Henry Quesenberry, Jr.**, was born on the 29th of July, 1863 — almost three months after his father's death — in Jonesville, Lee County, Virginia, where Rebecca had taken refuge with kin. The boy never met his father, and grew up in the household of his widowed teenage mother. Every Quesenberry descendant in Mike's line owes their existence to this young soldier who fell at Chancellorsville.

His regimental affiliation and burial site remain open research questions. Confederate dead at Chancellorsville were buried in mass graves on the battlefield; many were later moved to the Confederate Cemetery at Fredericksburg or to home cemeteries when families could afford to retrieve them. Whether Alexander Henry's body returned to Washington or Lee County, or rests still in the Wilderness woods, is unknown.

narrative: Isaac J. Harvey was born on the 29th of March, 1842 in North Carolina — by curious coincidence the same year as Pvt. Alexander Henry Quesenberry, Sr. He was a son of **Anthony Harvey** and **Sarah Sally Trueblood** — the Trueblood surname being a famous Quaker name from colonial Virginia and North Carolina, marking the deep Quaker roots of this Harvey line.

Isaac was a man much married. He buried two wives before he married Ruth's grandmother. His first wife was **Catherine Reich Harvey** (also spelled Rike). After her death he married her sister **Henrietta Annetta Reich Harvey** — a *sororate* marriage that was common in 19th-century rural America, where a widower would often marry his deceased wife's unmarried sister to keep the household and the in-laws intact. Henrietta too predeceased him. He then married, finally, **Rachel Frances Swift Harvey** — daughter of Thomas S. Harvey, and William Carl Harvey.

Isaac lived to seventy. He died on Friday, the 12th of April, 1912 — the day the RMS *Titanic* would sink off Newfoundland just three days later. He was buried in his Deep River community the next day, Saturday. The **Greensboro Daily News** of Saturday April 19, 1912, ran a brief community-news note from a correspondent: *'Isaac Harvey, an aged citizen living near here died Friday morning and was buried here Saturday.'* A modest valediction for a man who had outlived two wives, raised four children, and watched the nineteenth century give way to the twentieth.

narrative: Judith Deuce was born in 1683 in **Bilston, Staffordshire, England** — in what is now the Black Country of greater Wolverhampton, then a region of small ironworks, coal pits, and dissenting religious communities. Her father was **Samuel Deuce**; her mother **Elizabeth Deuce** (maiden name unrecovered). Bilston was a stronghold of early religious nonconformity — Quaker, Methodist, and Baptist congregations were all rooted there — and Judith almost certainly grew up in one of these dissenting families.

Sometime in the early 1700s — likely as a young woman or young wife — Judith joined the great migration of English Quakers and other nonconformists to **William Penn's Pennsylvania**. There she married first **Peter Osborne**, and with him bore at least five children: Elizabeth Ann (later Sheward), Charles, Peter, Suzanna, and Samuel Sr. After Peter Osborne's death she married, as her second husband, **William Harvey, I** — Mike's eighth-generation direct ancestor. With William she bore at least six more children: Hannah (later Way), William II, **Isaac L. Harvey** (born 1718 at Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania), James, Amos, and Anne (later Bayley).

Judith lived an extraordinarily long life — eighty-seven years across two marriages and at least eleven children. She died on the 1st of May, 1770, in **Chester, Pennsylvania** — still in the same Chester County Quaker community where her descendants would remain for another half-century before migrating south to Orange and Guilford Counties, North Carolina.
Judith is the deepest English-born ancestor in the Harvey line — pushing the documented Harvey ancestry back to the reign of Charles II and putting the family's origin firmly in the English Midlands.

narrative: Nathan Heaver Harvey was born on the 21st of September, 1759, in Chester County, Pennsylvania — the heart of William Penn's Quaker colony, where his Quaker forebears had settled in the late seventeenth century. He came of age during the American Revolution; at sixteen, when the war began, he would have been of fighting age, but as a Quaker his religious tradition would have led him to refuse military service. (Pennsylvania Quakers played a complex role in the Revolution: many refused arms; some were disowned by their meetings for fighting; others quietly supported the cause through hospital work, farming for the army, or simply continuing their lives.)

He married **Agnes Harvey** (1756–1834) — note the shared surname, suggesting either a cousin marriage or the convention of Quaker women keeping their birth surname. Together they raised at least one son, **Anthony Harvey** (born 23 April 1791, Alamance County, NC). Their move from Chester County PA to Orange County NC was part of the great Quaker migration south down the Great Wagon Road in the late eighteenth century — a migration that brought many Quaker families from Pennsylvania into the new Quaker settlements of Piedmont North Carolina (most famously the New Garden community in what became Guilford County).

Nathan died on the 12th of March, 1837, in Orange County, NC, age 77. His descendants would carry the Harvey name through five more American generations to William Carl Harvey (1887–1966) — Ruth's father.

narrative: Isaac L. Harvey was born on the 21st of September, 1718, at **Chadds Ford** in Chester County, Pennsylvania. The placename matters: Chadds Ford sits on the Brandywine Creek, on the road from Philadelphia to Wilmington. In September 1777 — when Isaac was 58 — that very ground would become the site of the **Battle of Brandywine**, the largest battle of the American Revolution measured by combatants engaged. George Washington's Continental Army would face Sir William Howe's British Regulars on Isaac's home soil. Whether he was still living there in 1777, or had already moved south to North Carolina, is uncertain. What is certain is that Chadds Ford was Quaker country — Brandywine Friends Meeting was one of the earliest in the colony.

He married **Martha E. Harvey** (born **Newlin**, 1721–1806), of the famous Pennsylvania Newlin Quaker family — daughter of Nathaniel Newlin (1690–1732) and Jane Newlin (b. 1687), the Irish Quaker emigrants who had come to Penn's colony in 1683 from Mountmellick, Ireland. Through this marriage the Harvey and Newlin Quaker lines joined.

They raised at least one son, **Nathan Heaver Harvey** (1759–1837), who would carry the family south to Orange County, North Carolina with the great Quaker migration down the Great Wagon Road. Isaac himself eventually made the same journey — he died on the 3rd of April, 1802, in Orange County, NC, age 83.

narrative: Riley James Mullins was born in 1838 in Claiborne County, Tennessee — into the great Mullins clan of the Cumberland Gap mountains. When the Civil War came he served the Confederacy. He was captured at some point and sent north to **Rock Island Prison Barracks**, a Union POW camp on an island in the Mississippi River between Illinois and Iowa. Rock Island was notorious for harsh conditions and high mortality from smallpox, dysentery, and exposure during the brutal winter of 1863–64. Of the roughly 12,000 Confederates held there, nearly 2,000 died.

Riley James was one of them — dead on the 16th of February, 1864, age 25. He was a cousin of Pvt. Alexander Henry Quesenberry, Sr. (killed at Chancellorsville May 1863), making this family's Confederate cost two young men dead within ten months of each other in the war's middle years.

narrative: Rhoda E. Pegram — daughter of an earlier-generation Pegram (parents not yet identified) — married **William Aydlott McMichael, Sr.** in Guilford County, North Carolina sometime around 1810–1815. Their son **Jesse C. McMichael** (b. 1820) would carry both family names forward, raising his own children in Deep River where the Pegrams and McMichaels lived side by side.

Rhoda is structurally one of the most important ancestors on the McMichael side. Through her, the Pegram surname enters this branch *two generations earlier* than through Sally Pegram (Geneva's mother). That means Geneva McMichael Harvey is descended from Pegrams along **two distinct lines** — Rhoda her great-great-grandmother (paternal), and Sally her mother. The Pegrams and McMichaels of Deep River were not merely neighbors who occasionally intermarried; they were a single extended kin-network whose descendants are often related two or three different ways.

narrative: Catherine "Rachel" Hutchins was born around 1703 in **Henrico, Virginia, British Colonial America** — to **Nicholas Hutchins** and **Mary Watkins**. She grew up in a large family of at least eleven siblings: Strangeman, Martha, Mary (later Harris), James, Carrie (later McNeal), John, Sarah, Benjamin, Elizabeth, Alice, and herself.

On the 5th of March, 1728, in Henrico, Virginia, she married **James Stanley, Sr.** Over the next two-plus decades they raised at least eight Stanley children: William, James Jr., **Mary Agnes** (Mike's gen-7 ancestor — who would later marry Anthony P. Hoggatt), Martha (later Thornburgh), Agnes (later Jessup), Strangeman (named for Catherine's brother), Elijah, and Micajah.

Sometime in the mid-eighteenth century the Stanley family migrated south from Virginia to North Carolina, joining the broader Quaker movement down the Great Wagon Road into the Piedmont. Catherine died on the 20th of December, 1766, in Guilford County, NC, and was buried at **New Garden Friends Monthly Meeting** — one of the foundational Quaker meetings of the Carolina Quaker community. New Garden would, over the next century, become the heart of the Friends presence in Piedmont NC and a center of antislavery sentiment.

Catherine is the deepest Hutchins-Stanley ancestor we have documented. Through her daughter Mary Agnes (later Hoggatt) the Stanley line merges into the Hoggatt-Newlin-Harvey lineage that leads down to Ruth Garland Harvey six generations later.
